newsitem.title: UK: Blair, Britain's Clinton, poised for victory.
newsitem.headline: Blair, Britain's Clinton, poised for victory.

text.p: Labour leader Tony Blair, a smooth-talking moderate who is ruthless with dissent, looks set to become Britain's youngest prime minister of the century after Thursday's election.
A child in the sixties, albeit no wild child, Blair would be the first British premier to be born after World War Two if his huge lead in the polls holds up. He is a tricky man to pin down.
A committed Christian, active father and archetypal "new man" in touch with his feelings and proud of his high-powered wife, 43-year-old Blair is no emotional softie.
For he is the politician who dared take on the entrenched leftist forces in his own party, root out vote-losing socialist policies and make Labour electable after 18 years in the cold.

His modernising instincts earned Blair some cruel nick-names -- Blur and Stalin both stuck for a while -- and voters never truly warmed to the man they considered both a clone of U.S. president Bill Clinton and a watered-down Conservative.
Like him or not, voters appear ready for a new start, especially the promise of a centrist new start.
"We do not promise a revolution. We promise only what we will deliver and we will deliver what we promise," Blair said in a typical soundbite during the six-week election campaign.
"We promise a government which can bring the country together, heal the divisions of the past and look to the future with confidence."
Voters say his policies often mirror those of the ruling Conservatives, but Blair looks very different from Prime Minister John Major, the "grey man" of British politics.

While Major is a working class boy made good at the top of a Conservative party built on wealth and privilege, Blair -- unlike most Labour men -- was groomed for success at the best of private schools.
He has lived a life untouched by world war in a nation that sets great store by its victory over fascism.
This former band leader, pure Mick Jagger in style if not in talent, freely admits: "I am from the rock and roll generation."
Like Clinton he went to Oxford University. Like Clinton, he comes from the moderate wing of his party and is distrusted by the old party faithful. Unlike Clinton, he neither smoked drugs nor inhaled.
Blair is not the sort to share beer and sandwiches with the trade unionists who for so long held Labour in a vice-like grip, although he does enjoy a pint and takeaway fish and chips.
Like Clinton, he married a woman with strong political views who is more than his equal -- Cherie Booth is one of the top lawyers of her generation.
A die-hard centrist, Blair is religious: a man his spin-doctors say can be trusted by a nation leery of the left.
"He is the worst thing that could happen to us," a Conservative minister once confessed.
Nobody could have guessed as much before the sudden death of populist Labour leader John Smith in 1994 paved the way for Blair's rise from virtual obscurity.
Indeed, the Daily Telegraph had once damned Blair as "too nice and too unguarded to be a politician".
Anthony Charles Lynton Blair was born in Edinburgh in 1953, the son of an aspiring Conservative politician.
He was brought up in the northeast of England and remains the representative at Westminster for his old Sedgefield home.

Aged 11, Blair stood as the Conservative candidate in a mock school election and it was not until university that he showed any inclination towards the left. "I just wasn't interested. I had no thought of going into parliament," he said.
Educated at an exclusive Scottish private school in Edinburgh, he read law at Oxford and went on to become a barrister in London specialising in trade union law.
Aged 14, he tried to flee the country rather than return to his strict private school, Fettes, dubbed the Eton of Scotland.
"It was one of the craziest things I've ever done," he said recently of his abortive attempt to visit the Bahamas.
At Oxford, Blair's rebellious streak continued as he fronted a rock band called "The Ugly Rumours", grew his hair long and dressed up in garish 1970s fashions.
But his mind was really on other things as the man who would be Labour's youngest leader embraced socialism and Christianity.
"Blair was essentially a rather sensible young man. Discreet about sex, abstemious about drugs and earnest about rock 'n' roll," said John Rentoul, Blair's biographer.
This sensible streak served him well.

In 1983, Blair won a safe Labour seat and began his speedy rise through the party ranks, speaking as opposition Treasury spokesman, formulating party policy on the trade unions and tackling the tricky home-affairs portfolio.

When Smith died, Blair was by no means the automatic choice to succeed him. Gordon Brown, the party's economics spokesman and Smith's right-hand man, looked the logical choice and Brown and Blair thrashed it out as friends and rivals.
It was the fresh-faced Blair who won -- so fresh-faced that none of his inner circle has experience of office.

Blair is not fazed. Dismissed first as a man who didn't know his mind -- Blur -- then one who imposed his will ruthlessly -- Stalin -- Blair has found his footing and can now joke about the tags earned along the way.
"It has been hard, I know. Hard for me sometimes," he said at one Labour Party Conference. "Last year Bambi, this year Stalin. From Disneyland to dictatorship in twelve short months."

Even allies say he is petulant under fire and has a tendency to exaggerate setbacks. But he also shares a doggedness that served Margaret Thatcher so well -- and the same will to succeed that ensured she governed Britain for 11 years.

"Thatcher is his model. And she once said that her single greatest success was the change she had brought about in the Labour Party. That's also Tony Blair's job -- in reverse, of course," said Jonathan Powell, Blair's chief of staff.
